As the son of a well-known, sometimes controversial politician, I am sometimes asked: how was your dad like a man, how did you experience him within the family context? And sometimes more directly: Was he really such a dogmatic "man of granite" like the media portrays him?

My answer is no, in reality he was a very approachable but at the same time principled person with the special ability to lead through a well-considered, reasoned styke of debating. He was a true visionary with a special vision for the future of South-Africa as a country of many peoples, where every population group would have a similar extent of freedom and autonomy in its own teritory without being suppressed by any other group. He was convinced that this would be the only way in which the historical problems of mutual struggle and exploitation could be solved, and has taken every opportunity to proclaim this ideal.

But he was not a dreamer, and had the ability to turn his vision into practical steps, sometimes under great opposition. Did he, as a father, force his convictions upon his children? People are usually surprised when I say that at home we seldom discusses politics. My father strongly took the stance that we, as children, should find our own paths, and develop independent opinions. He was, however, always available to answer questions, to defend stances, and to argue.

As a father he was strict, but always righteous when we had made errors, yet always unimpeachable whenever principles were involved. This can be illustrated well by an incident that involved me as a young student at the UP (Univeristy of Pretoria).

I was fairly well involved in students' politics, and at one point chairman of the UP's Afrikaanse Studentebondtak (Afrikaner Students Affiliation). One day we received a letter from the USA from a student that said he was interested in our political system, and had planned to visit South Africa and visit various population groups and research their stances.

We considered this as a good opportunity to defend our country and we even invited him to spend a few days in Sonop, the hostel where I lived. A few months later he turns up, is met with hospitality and lead around, yet he disappoints us with a lack of real interest and he doesn't let us hear anything from him afterwards.

A few weeks later I get a call that I should urgently go see my father. I get to hear that the security police are investigating into a matter against me. It turns out that this "friend" of mine was caught at the the border with Botswana with an ANC activist wanted by the police hidden in the truk of his car, and it is apparently not the first time he smuggled someone across the border. They also find my invation letter on him, which he used to abtain a visum, having planned everything well.

My father was of course very upset and the first thing that he told me, was that I had to clearly understand that if I were guilty, he wouldn't move a finger to help me, and that I would have to undergo the full penalty of law.

I had to make a statement to the security police and defend it to the Minister of Foreign Affairs. Luckily they all accepted my explanation. Only later I learned that this American was a well-known leftist activist and that the police were already on his track.

For me this was an important lesson to never blindly trust people. More important however, this was an affirmation of my father's impeachable rejection of any form of corruption or nepotism.
